blocks.tk: Magtymguly 18-nji asyrda türkmen edebiýatynyň ýoluny açypdyr. 19-njy asyrda bu ýoly başga şahyrlar dowam etdiripdirler. Olaryň arasynda iki şahyryň ady aýratyn meşhur: Kemine we Mollanepes. Kemine adalatsyzlygy tankytlaýan şahyr, Mollanepes bolsa söýgi baradaky goşgulary we dessany bilen tanalýar.
blocks.en: Magtymguly opened the way in the 18th century; in the 19th, other poets followed it. Two of them are especially loved: Kemine and Mollanepes. In Britannica's words, both carried the styles and themes of the 18th century into the 19th: Kemine as a sharp social critic, Mollanepes as the author of the epic *Zöhre-Tahyr*.

blocks.tk: Keminäniň hakyky ady Mämmetweli. Ol takmynan 1770-nji ýylda Saragtda garyp bir maşgalada doglupdyr. Ilki Saragtda bir molladan okapdyr, soňra Buharadaky medresede bilim alypdyr. Ol 1840-njy ýyllarda aradan çykypdyr. Onuň “Kemine” diýen lakamy “kiçigöwünli” diýmekdir. Çeşmeleriň aýtmagyna görä, onuň kyrka golaý goşgusy biziň günlerimize çenli gelipdir.
blocks.en: Kemine's real name was Mämmetweli. He was born around 1770 in Sarahs, into a poor family, studied first with a mullah in Sarahs and then at a madrasa in Bukhara, and died around 1840. His pen name is usually explained as **the humble one**. Some forty of his poems survive, according to Wikipedia and to the scholars who have studied them, along with about a hundred humorous stories told about him.

blocks.tk: Kemine garyplaryň durmuşy barada köp ýazypdyr. Onuň goşgularynda baýlary, para alýan kazylary we ikiýüzli mollalary tankytlaýan setirler köp. Ol pikirini baýlaryň öňünde hem gorkman aýdypdyr. Şonuň üçin ol halkyň söýýän şahyry bolupdyr. Kemine barada degişmeler hem köp: olarda ol hemişe garyp, ýöne güýçlilerden has akylly adam. Bu degişmeleri özbekler we gazaklar hem bilýärler. Onuň “Garyplyk” atly goşgusy şu bent bilen gutarýar:
blocks.en: Kemine wrote about the lives of the poor, and many of his lines mock the rich, judges who take bribes and hypocritical clerics; one of his best-known satires is addressed to a judge who sells false verdicts. Turkmen tell many short humorous stories about him, in which he is always poor and always cleverer than the powerful, and scholars have compared him with Nasreddin Hodja; the stories are known among Uzbeks, Kazakhs and Kyrgyz as well. His poem “Garyplyk”, **Poverty**, ends with this stanza:

blocks.tk: Kemine diýr, geler bir gün şum ölüm, / Kimsäge — toý-baýram, kimsäge — zulum, / Gyýylma, ynjama, sabr eýle, köňlüm! / Gelipdir, bir zaman öter garyplyk.
blocks.en: Kemine says: one day grim death will come; / for some it is a feast, for others, cruelty. / Don't grieve, don't be hurt, be patient, my heart! / Poverty has come; one day it will pass.
blocks.source: Kemine, “Garyplyk”, last stanza, early 19th century; text as in Kemine, Goşgular (Aşgabat: Turan, 1991); our translation

blocks.tk: Mollanepesiň hakyky ady Nepes. Ol takmynan 1810-njy ýylda Saragtyň golaýynda doglupdyr. Ilki Maryda, soňra Buharada we Hywada okapdyr. Ol 1862-nji ýylda Marynyň golaýynda aradan çykypdyr, ýöne käbir çeşmelerde başga sene görkezilýär. Onuň goşgularynda şekiller köp, dili bolsa baý. Mollanepesiň söýgi baradaky goşgularyny bagşylar häzir hem aýdýarlar.
blocks.en: Mollanepes, Nepes son of Kadyrberdi, was born around 1810 near Sarahs and studied in Mary and then, according to Wikipedia, in Bukhara and Khiva. He died in 1862 near Mary, though the Great Russian Encyclopedia notes that other accounts give around 1875. His love lyrics, rich in images and in language, are still sung by bagşys.

blocks.tk: Onuň iň meşhur eseri “Zöhre-Tahyr” dessany. Bu dessan şanyň gyzy Zöhre bilen Tahyryň söýgüsi barada. Şa sözünden dänýär we iki ýaş aşygy biri-birinden aýyrýar. Bu gadymy hekaýany köp halk bilýär: türkmenler, özbekler, azerbaýjanlar, tatarlar we başgalar. Dessanda söýgi, wepalylyk we ykbal barada köp pikir bar. Onuň dürli görnüşleri bar, olaryň ahyry hem dürli. Mollanepes bu hekaýany goşgy we kyssa bilen täzeden ýazypdyr.
blocks.en: His best-known work is the *dessan* (epic) *Zöhre-Tahyr*, on what Britannica calls a medieval folk theme: the love of Zöhre, a shah's daughter, and Tahyr, whom the shah, breaking his word, keeps from her. The tale is told across the Turkic world, among Uzbeks, Azerbaijanis, Tatars and others, in many versions with different endings, all turning on love, loyalty and fate; in the Anatolian version described by the TDV encyclopedia, the lovers die. Mollanepes retold it in Turkmen verse and prose, giving its characters, as his biographers note, a new depth.

blocks.tk: Çeşmeler iki şahyryň dost bolandygyny ýazýarlar. Häzir Türkmenistanda olaryň adyny göterýän köçeler bar. Marydaky teatr Keminäniň adyny göterýär, Mary welaýatyndaky bir şäher bolsa Mollanepesiň adyny göterýär. Okuwçylar olaryň goşgularyny mekdepde okaýarlar.
blocks.en: The two poets knew each other: a Turkmen account and a scholarly article both describe Kemine as a close friend of Mollanepes. Today streets in Turkmenistan bear their names; the theatre in Mary is named after Kemine, and a town in Mary province after Mollanepes. Their poems are part of the school curriculum.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Look for this unit's grammar: the genitive doer in *halkyň söýýän şahyry* (the poet the people love), *-dYgY* in *iki şahyryň dost bolandygyny ýazýarlar* (write that the two poets were friends), and the participles in *para alýan kazylar* (judges who take bribes) and *adyny göterýän köçeler*. The poem is in an older literary style: *diýr* for *diýýär*, *eýle* for *et*.
